output.headline: Care workers win exception from toughest new settlement rules
output.bodyHtml:
Shabana Mahmood has granted care workers an exemption from her toughest settlement rules, after a cabinet backlash and pressure from health unions secured a carve-out allowing them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. The home secretary rowed back from her original plan to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that most other migrants would still face retrospective rule changes making them wait a decade.

The key climbdown was the exemption for care workers, something the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, had also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.

Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. In the revised proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.

But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood's office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement.

Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement. She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”

Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years. For those earning under £50,000, the wait will double to 10 years, which was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.

Home Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood's softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.

The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds. Refugees will otherwise face a wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.

Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood's migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”

Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.

Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn't unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”

The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”. The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood's decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.

Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.

Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.

The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.

Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone's plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I'll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”

The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.

The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”. She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don't claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”

Migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government's requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families' lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.

Business groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.

Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.
output.standfirst: Health union pressure has won care workers and their dependants an exception allowing them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, as most other migrants face a decade-long wait for settlement
output.progress: Mahmood met union leaders and granted care workers a carve-out, after sustained pressure from cabinet colleagues and unions.

output.headline: Burnham to ask Commonwealth countries to help shape UK's slavery apology
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham will ask countries affected by Britain’s role in slavery to help shape an expected formal apology, Downing Street has indicated, arguing that their input is indispensable in crafting an enduring message.

The prime minister was en route to the Commonwealth heads of government summit (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda, which begins on Tuesday. No 10 said he would use the event to launch a “structured dialogue” into what form an apology might take.

Downing Street has ruled out the idea of paying reparations after an apology, but Burnham is expected to set out plans at the summit for a system of debt restructuring for countries facing higher debt costs.

UK officials already at the summit said other Commonwealth countries had responded positively to the move, and that it could help talks on separate issues such as trade and the climate.

In comments released by No 10 before Burnham’s arrival, the prime minister said discussion of an apology marked a new approach towards the UK’s relations with the Commonwealth.

“In today’s more divided, unpredictable world, the Commonwealth has the potential to be a powerful force for good, bringing together a third of the global population, and I believe it is key that the UK plays its full role in that,” Burnham said.

“Britain is bringing a new approach to this meeting as we look to reshape a new era for the Commonwealth, as well as being open to discussions about the past.”

Burnham set out his intention to look at a possible apology in an article for the Guardian on Saturday, in which he said the UK should “show leadership again today” as it had done in efforts to end the transatlantic slave trade.

Asked why Burnham believed an apology was needed, his official spokesperson said: “The prime minister wants to strengthen the Commonwealth as a family of nations with shared values that can support growth around the world through trade and economic collaboration.” Having conversations about an apology would do this, and was also the right thing to do, he said.

Tony Blair expressed “deep sorrow” about the slave trade and Britain’s role in it in 2006, but stopped short of a formal apology.

Burnham intended to go further, his spokesperson said. “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognised the way it still shapes our world today.

Related: Monday briefing: The world is demanding reparations for enslavement – is Britain finally listening?

“That is distinct from a formal apology. We are opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade, and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.

“We think it’s right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take. An apology of this significance should be informed by the people and countries most affected, as they have asked for.”

Burnham is scheduled to take part in a series of assemblies at Chogm, as well as bilateral meetings with other leaders.

There was no single event set aside to discuss slavery or an apology, but discussions would take place “throughout the next couple of days”, No 10 said, adding that the Foreign Office would lead talks over the form of an apology.

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is already at the summit. One Foreign Office official said other Commonwealth countries “are responding positively to our offer of a structured dialogue” on an apology.

“The conversations at Chogm have been focused on the positive work this alliance can do together on issues like climate and trade,” they said. “By not shying away from difficult discussions about our past, we are building trust with our allies to focus on the big issues of the future.”

No 10 denied that Burnham’s comments had potentially embarrassed King Charles, who is already in Antigua and Barbuda for a pre-Chogm visit.

Buckingham Palace “was made aware in a timely manner”, Burnham’s spokesperson said. “The prime minister believes that being true to British values of decency and honesty means not shying away from these conversations.”
output.standfirst: Andy Burnham will launch a 'structured dialogue' on a possible apology at the Commonwealth summit in Antigua and Barbuda, as No 10 rules out paying reparations for Britain's role in the slave trade
output.progress: Burnham has launched a structured dialogue with Commonwealth countries to help shape a possible formal apology, and plans a debt-restructuring scheme for struggling nations.

output.headline: Vance says US and Iran have 'made some progress' towards a deal
output.bodyHtml:
US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction, hours before the US launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, according to reports in US media.

“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”

Vance’s comments came after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington over a deal with Iran. If confirmed, the Qeshm strikes would mark the first publicly known attack by the US on Iran in weeks.

The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.

When asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.

Related: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war

Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy. “There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”

Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices that came as his administration touted renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections, with polls showing voters likely to punish Republicans for the effect on the cost of living.

Several explosions were heard on Qeshm Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear. The strikes – first reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) – targeted surface to air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

US Central Command did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency, and the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that have not been made public.

The paper said that sources suggested the recent strikes have been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.

The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.

Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.
output.standfirst: The US reportedly carried out limited 'defensive' strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, after Iranian state media reported hearing explosions in the strait of Hormuz, on the eve of crucial US midterm elections
output.progress: Vice-president JD Vance says he and Trump feel positive about reaching a negotiated settlement with Iran.

context.text: JD Vance sent Iran's security council secretary a personal letter on Sunday, after Qatari mediation, offering to restart diplomacy to avert a fresh conflict.

output.headline: Charges dropped against Olympic canoeist wrongly blamed for pool damage
output.bodyHtml:
Prosecutors have dropped the case against David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist who was initially charged over alleged damage to Donald Trump’s $14m renovation of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. Trump had alleged that vandals were to blame for the pool’s problems, although his administration failed to produce evidence to substantiate the claims; the office of the US attorney, Jeanine Pirro, later dropped the case against Hearn, infuriating the president.

Hearn’s attorneys said the case’s dismissal “does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong”.

Donald Trump unveiled the delayed results of the renovation in what is expected to be his final press conference before voters head to the polls for the midterm elections.

On the eve of a consequential election day, with polls indicating that most voters feel the US president has grown too focused on building projects in the nation’s capital, he stood in front of the newly opened reflecting pool to discuss – in detail – changes to the pool’s pipe, the grass surrounding the area and granite.

“This project should be a project that unites all Americans,” Trump told reporters on Monday afternoon.

It has proven anything but. After Trump’s first revealed his “beautiful” makeover of the reflecting pool in June, a massive algae bloom turned it green (instead of the promised “American flag blue”) and the coating started to peel away.

On Monday, Trump accused his Democratic predecessors, Joe Biden and Barack Obama, of overspending on previous renovations to the reflecting pool and once again, without evidence, accused vandals of purposefully damaging the Trump administration’s renovations.

Roughly 20 minutes into his remarks on the reflecting pool, less than 24 hours before Americans head to the polls, Trump pivoted to acknowledge Tuesday’s midterm elections, which he declared to be crucial.

The party of a sitting president often loses seats during the midterms, he noted. “We gave this a very strong shot,” Trump said.

For weeks, polls have shown Democratic candidates are narrowly ahead of Republican candidates in key races – that includes competitive Senate races in Texas, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa and Maine.

Voters have expressed dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of his job as president, particularly over the US economy and cost of living.

The prices of gas and groceries have risen since the beginning of the year, and inflation has remained stubbornly high – largely the result of the war with Iran that Trump started at the end of February.
output.standfirst: Trump unveiled the delayed $14m reflecting pool renovation in his final midterms press conference, after an algae bloom turned the pool green and its coating peeled away
output.progress: Prosecutors dropped the case against David Hearn, the Olympic canoeist wrongly accused of vandalising the pool.

output.headline: Kristin Scott Thomas stars as a glamorous granny in John Lewis's 20th Christmas ad
output.bodyHtml:
John Lewis has cast an actor best known for playing aristocrats to bring a playful, upmarket spin to this year's countdown to Christmas, with a festive ad starring a talking toy dog called Pickles and a glamorous granny.

Kristin Scott Thomas, known for upper-crust roles in films such as Four Weddings and a Funeral and the Apple TV show Slow Horses, plays Gloria, a grandmother on the hunt for gift inspiration, under the tagline “don’t give up on giving”.

Now in its 20th year, the department store's blockbuster Christmas ad kicks off the official countdown with Pickles, voiced by the comedian Paul Whitehouse, challenging Gloria to “do better than cash” when choosing a gift for her grandchildren.

Pickles drags Gloria out of the house on a last-minute mission to find gifts, and after rejecting options in other shops, she sets off on a magical tuk-tuk ride to John Lewis, where she snaps up disco balls and fairy lights to create a “gran cave” to hang out with her grandchildren, Freddie and Maggie.

Rosie Hanley, the marketing director of John Lewis, said the retailer had increased its spend on this year's festive ad as the cost of production had risen, and that it wanted to “push the boat out” for its 20th year.

She said the company was nonetheless confident it would see “a really strong return on our investment”, as it looks to grab shoppers' attention ahead of the Black Friday discount period later this month.

Hanley said John Lewis had wanted the ad “to be more joyful” this year because “things are tough for lots of families”. Despite concerns among British households about higher energy bills and housing costs, she said spending on Christmas-related gear at John Lewis was already running ahead of last year.

The ad, set to a Sam Fender version of the Rolling Stones song You Can’t Always Get What You Want, features a range of John Lewis products in different price brackets, including the £12.99 Fisher-Price pull-along toy dog and a £255 Weekend Max Mara top and matching £290 skirt worn by Gloria.

The three-minute ad will launch on social media on Tuesday morning, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and YouTube, before a 60-second version airs for the first time on TV in the ad breaks for ITV's Coronation Street and Channel 4's The Great British Bake Off on Tuesday evening.

John Lewis will also erect a giant Christmas tree outside its store on London's Oxford Street to mark the recent pedestrianisation of the road. The company said the numbers of visitors to its store on the street last week were up by more than a fifth on the same week last year.

This year's ad, created by the Saatchi & Saatchi agency, returns to a formula of using a cute character – such as Monty the penguin in 2014 and Buster the boxer in 2016 – after two years foregrounding other family relationships. However, it has the twist of focusing on the relationship between Pickles and a grandmother rather than centring on cute children.

Hanley said the ad was inspired by research which had revealed that 52% of grandparents give cash as presents because they are not sure what youngsters really want. “People want to give thoughtful gifts but can often lack confidence, so resort to giving cash,” she said.

Now considered a national moment which invites social media comment and skits, the first big-budget John Lewis festive TV ad launched in 2007, soundtracked by a piece of music by Prokofiev.

Previous John Lewis Christmas TV ads have been soundtracked by covers including the Smiths song Please, Please, Please, Let Me Get What I Want and Together in Electric Dreams by Giorgio Moroder and Philip Oakey. Last year's ad included the 1990s club classic Where Love Lives by Alison Limerick.

This year's track, which features the choir from the John Spence community high school, which Fender previously attended, and the Easington Colliery Band, will be released on vinyl later this month, with proceeds going to Action For Children. Pickles the dog is based on an existing Fisher-Price pull-along toy called Little Snoopy that is celebrating its 60th year.

The John Lewis ad launch comes hot on the heels of other festive ads for most of the big supermarkets that kicked off last weekend. Total ad spending across the festive period is set to reach £14bn, up 8.2% year-on-year according to the annual review by the Advertising Association and research group WARC. That growth is led by an 18.5% year-on-year surge in social media spend, while total TV spending is expected to be up by 1.6%.
output.standfirst: The department store's latest festive ad features a talking toy dog called Pickles, as John Lewis marks 20 years of blockbuster Christmas advertising with a call to 'do better than cash'

output.headline: AI is already helping experts catch critical security flaws before hackers can exploit them
output.bodyHtml:
Artificial intelligence is already helping cybersecurity experts catch dangerous flaws before attackers can exploit them: last month, AI helped uncover a critical weakness in PHP, the computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites. But AI-powered malicious software is also “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body.

Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said the warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology. “AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance.

“It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC.

The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks.

Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states.

After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils.

AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC.

Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.

NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently.

“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say.

Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”.

Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”.

Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”.

Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience.

“For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.
output.standfirst: The National Cyber Security Centre says AI-powered malware is highly likely to be used in a ransomware attack on UK power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028
output.progress: Leading AI firms including OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advance access to help identify serious security flaws before attackers do.

output.headline: EHRC presses Reform UK to explain how it is complying with the Equality Act
output.bodyHtml:
The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it had written to Nigel Farage’s party in the wake of revelations in ITV’s Undercover: A Year in Reform, which was broadcast in October.

The official equalities watchdog raised concerns after the undercover TV documentary showed councillors and candidates for the party expressing racist and misogynistic views, with one of the party’s MPs complaining about ingrained sexism.

An EHRC statement said its letter had asked Reform to provide information, “including what action the party is taking to comply with the Equality Act”.

In the wake of the documentary, the statement said, the EHRC “received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns about racial and sexual remarks expressed by councillors, prospective councillors and members”.

It went on: “As with every complaint we receive, we will assess the information provided carefully and, following that consideration, take action where appropriate.

“Political parties, like all duty-bearers, must comply with the Equality Act and take steps to avoid discrimination or harassment including on the grounds of race, religion or belief and sex. We have guidance advising parties on their responsibilities under the act and urge them to consider it. This could include reviewing party policies or practices to identify areas of potential discrimination, harassment or victimisation that need to be addressed.”

While Farage has said the party’s vetting procedures have improved greatly, footage in the programme included Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites”, making Islamophobic remarks, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”.

Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues.

In another section, the Reform MP Sarah Pochin was shown complaining that the party was “chauvinistic” and riven with “alpha male shit”.

It comes weeks after the EHRC wrote to the Greens in England and Wales to seek more information about a new party policy which equates Zionism with racism and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state.

Reform has said it reported ITV and the reporters concerned to police, with separate threats of civil legal action against the broadcaster.

Responding to the EHRC letter, a party spokesperson said: “We are confident we have fully complied with our obligations under the Equality Act. There is no room for racism in Reform UK.”
output.standfirst: The equalities watchdog has written to Nigel Farage's party after an undercover documentary showed councillors and candidates making racist and misogynistic remarks, including one calling for the King to be killed
output.progress: The EHRC has asked Reform UK what action it is taking to comply with the Equality Act, and will assess the complaints it received.

output.headline: 'It's really, really unusual': a bull and donkey's tender bond baffles scientists
output.bodyHtml:
In Greek myth, Achilles and Patroclus were two heroes of the Trojan war whose intense bond some believed had turned into a sexual relationship.

In modern science, they are a bull, Achille, and a donkey, Patroclo, whose tender interspecies affair is helping to shed new light on social and sexual interactions between animals.

Researchers observed the two males licking and rubbing each other, with the bull sometimes mounting the donkey.

The team said while other donkeys attempted to avoid Achille’s attentions and showed threatening facial expressions towards him, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nibbled him.

“It is really, really unusual,” said Dr Elisabetta Palagi of the University of Pisa in Italy, who co-authored the study. “And it is the first time it is reported in literature.”

André da Cruz, a PhD student at the University of Pisa and another author, said the relationship was discovered by accident while the researchers were studying geladas, or bleeding-heart monkeys, in Ethiopia.

“We were having a little break for lunch, and in the distance I see something – it seemed a bit odd,” said da Cruz. “I told colleagues: ‘I think I saw a bull mounting a donkey.’ And they didn’t believe me.”

Writing in the journal Current Biology, the researchers said the bull and the donkey belonged to different owners and only came into contact with each other when, as part of their daily routine, their herds used the same pasture.

The researchers studied Achille and Patroclo over four days when they were both grazing in the same area, and four days when only one was present.

The team recorded 51 mountings of Patroclo by Achille, and noted that licking and rubbing often occurred both before and, more surprisingly, after such events.

“Rather than being solely attributable to sexual arousal, these interactions appear to play a role in prolonging the social interaction beyond the sexual act,” they wrote.

Despite ample opportunity, neither Achille nor Patroclo tried to mount a member of their own species of either sex, although Achille did show courtship behaviours towards some female cattle.

Related: Animal homosexual behaviour under-reported by scientists, survey shows

Such interspecies encounters are rare, but there have been other examples, including a male snow monkey attempting to have sex with a female sika deer, and an Antarctic fur seal that not only sexually harassed king penguins but engaged in necrophilia.

However, Palagi said there was no indication that the relationship between the donkey and the bull involved force.

“We interpret our data as a special relationship,” Palagi said, adding that the two males searched for each other. “When Achille approached someone else in the plateau, Patroclo went to him and tried to distract him,” she said.

Da Cruz said the mounting behaviour of Achille was unlikely to simply be a case of the bull exerting dominance.

“We saw on several occasions what might have been semen from the bull, or he might have been orgasming, although we cannot verify [that] completely,” da Cruz said, adding that Patroclo was highly aggressive to bulls other than Achille.

Palagi added that the relationship was an example of a sexual interaction that was disentangled from reproductive function.

“When two individuals belonging to the same species or different species need to develop a special relationship, they fish simply from their entire [behavioural] repertoire,” she said.

Palagi said it was unclear whether the sexual and social relationship between Patroclo and Achille had always co-existed or if one had led to the other. But, she added, the bond appeared to bring benefits, both in terms of attention but potentially also support.

Josh Luke Davis, the author of A Little Gay Natural History, said interspecies relationships were not necessarily unusual and that the widespread and common nature of queer behaviours in the natural world meant it was “probably not that surprising” that they overlapped.

“There is obviously value in reporting these kinds of behaviours,” Davis added. “But I would caution against reading too much into the significance of it and would be concerned about how it could be misconstrued or twisted by those who already deem homosexuality ‘unnatural’.”
output.standfirst: Patroclo the donkey and Achille the bull's interspecies affair is shedding new light on social and sexual relations between animals, scientists say
output.progress: Scientists are continuing to study the pair's unusual bond to better understand social and sexual behaviour across species.
